claims.text: The support index page links to /docs/support/provider-support-policy/, and a page exists at that path in the Pulumi docs.
The Pulumi docs page at /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ describes how long Pulumi maintains each provider major version.
Pulumi provides long-term security updates for some providers (but not all), and the provider support policy page identifies which providers get them.
Pulumi maintains each provider major version for a defined period of time under its provider support policy.
Pulumi does not automatically roll back changes made during an update if an error or failure occurs; it completes any pending in-progress operations, then exits and reports the error.
To perform a manual rollback after a failed Pulumi deployment, you revert the code and configuration changes and run `pulumi up` to return infrastructure to its previous state.

Pulumi does not automatically query the cloud provider's live state before running `pulumi up` or `pulumi preview`; it compares the desired state declared in the program against the last recorded state to determine changes.

Refreshing state requires a round-trip to the cloud provider for every resource in a stack, which adds significant latency, especially for large stacks; not refreshing automatically before every update is an intentional Pulumi design decision.
Running `pulumi refresh` synchronizes Pulumi's recorded state with the actual state of the cloud resources.
`pulumi up --refresh` refreshes state and applies the desired state in a single step.
Pulumi Cloud provides built-in drift detection for automated drift detection and remediation on a schedule.
The page /docs/deployments/concepts/drift/ exists and covers Pulumi Cloud drift detection.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/state-and-backends/ has a 'Refreshing state' section explaining refresh behavior in detail.
In Pulumi, the logical name of a resource is part of the auto-assigned resource URN, while the physical name is how the resource is known to the cloud provider.
A Pulumi resource's logical name only needs to be unique within a stack, while the physical name typically needs to be unique within a certain scope (sometimes globally).
Pulumi auto-naming creates each resource's physical name by combining the logical name with a random suffix appended afterwards.
Pulumi's auto-naming with random suffixes lets Pulumi replace resources with less downtime, by creating the replacement before deleting the old resource.
An auto-named Pulumi resource's physical name will typically look like `my-bucket-d7c2fa0` (logical name plus a 7-character random hex suffix) instead of `my-bucket`.
Auto-naming can be disabled on a per-resource basis, which gives precise physical names without random suffixes but loses the benefits of side-by-side stacks and reduced-downtime replacement.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has an 'autonaming' section.
Project or stack configuration can be used to customize or disable auto-naming globally, per provider, or per resource type.
The page /docs/iac/concepts/resources/names/ has an 'Auto-naming Configuration' (autonaming-configuration) section.
During a Pulumi update, secrets are decrypted in memory and visible to the Pulumi program.
Pulumi provides primitives to store secrets securely in the CLI, state file, and Pulumi Cloud.
Passing `--secret` to `pulumi config set` causes the configuration value to be encrypted so it can be safely persisted in `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml`.
Pulumi Cloud manages a unique encryption key for every stack, used to encrypt that stack's secrets, and this is configurable to use a custom secrets provider.

Because a different encryption key is used per stack, encrypting the same value in two different stacks produces different encrypted strings in the `Pulumi.<stack-name>.yaml` files, so an encrypted value cannot be copied between files with a text editor and `pulumi config set` must be used instead.

When running a preview, update, or destroy, Pulumi decrypts secret config data; it is plain text during deployment execution and any part of the Pulumi program can access it using the Pulumi config object.
Pulumi does not use the Terraform engine in any way.
Some Pulumi providers use the open-source Terraform schemas to determine available resources and parameters and to determine return and response attributes.
Pulumi native providers are mapped directly to the cloud provider APIs and do not use Terraform schemas.
The blog post /blog/pulumiup-native-providers/ exists and the external Terraform schemas link (https://www.terraform.io/docs/extend/schemas/index.html) resolves.
Pulumi is a declarative tool that uses imperative languages to define the end state; the language is used for authoring the program and not for talking to the cloud provider API.
Pulumi uses strongly typed programming languages that support IntelliSense and the Language Server Protocol, so when defining Pulumi programs you rarely need to leave your IDE.
Experimental Pulumi features are always opt-in, enabled explicitly with a flag, command, or environment variable (such as `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true`).
The `PULUMI_EXPERIMENTAL=true` environment variable enables experimental functionality in the Pulumi CLI.
Experimental Pulumi features are not necessarily supported and can change or be removed at any time without a deprecation cycle.
When an experimental feature proves valuable, Pulumi invests in stabilizing it and promoting it to general availability.
Pulumi focuses on actively supporting the latest released major version of the providers it maintains.
For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi also ships security updates for the previous major version for up to a year, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The provider support policy page (/docs/support/provider-support-policy/) lists the covered providers and what a long-term support release contains.
Older major versions of Pulumi-maintained providers (beyond the latest major, and beyond the security-update window for previous major of widely used providers) receive no patches at all.
The Pulumi Registry (/registry/) lists the current version for all providers maintained by Pulumi.
Major provider versions typically include significant changes such as deprecations, new resources and new functionality, which may require additional migration steps.
Minor provider versions typically include new resources and features, performance improvements, and bug fixes without introducing breaking changes.
Each provider release has release notes summarizing new capabilities or fixes.
In npm, the tilde operator (e.g. `~1.2.3`) allows patch updates on the current minor version.
Provider patch versions are primarily for bug fixes and security updates and are designed to be fully backward compatible.

Each major version of a Pulumi provider includes migration logic to smooth the upgrade from the immediately previous major version, but these migrations do not always work across multiple major versions.
Pulumi recommends updating to the latest minor version on the current major provider version at least quarterly.
Pulumi recommends never being 2 major provider versions behind, since jumping a major version is inadvisable due to potential breaking changes.
The page /docs/support/provider-support-policy/ exists and is the Provider support policy.
Pages /docs/support/faq/secrets-config/ (Pulumi ESC FAQ), /docs/support/faq/pulumi-cloud/ (Pulumi Cloud FAQ), and /docs/support/faq/policies/ (Pulumi Policies FAQ) exist.
Pulumi actively maintains the latest released major version of every provider it publishes.

For a set of widely used providers, Pulumi ships security updates for the previous major version for up to 12 months after the next major release, or until the next major version is released, whichever comes first.
The providers that receive long-term support updates on eligible older versions are: AWS, Azure Classic, Azure Native, Azure AD, Command, Docker Build, GCP, Kubernetes, TLS, and Vault.
The Pulumi Registry has package pages at /registry/packages/aws/, azure/, azure-native/, azuread/, command/, docker-build/, gcp/, kubernetes/, tls/, and vault/.
The LTS branch of a covered Pulumi provider ships High/Critical CVE security patches.
LTS releases include fixes for CVEs affecting the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
LTS releases include fixes for broken internal infrastructure on the LTS branch needed to ship the CVE security patches.

An LTS release of a Pulumi provider does not contain new upstream API versions, new resources or new resource properties, performance improvements, non-security bug fixes, or compatibility with newer versions of language runtimes.
LTS providers remain compatible with the version of the Pulumi engine they were frozen at, unless security fixes require otherwise.
Under Pulumi's provider support policy, exactly one long-term support major version exists per covered provider at any time.
When major version N+1 of a covered Pulumi provider ships, it becomes the new N, and the old N becomes the new LTS major.
When a new major version of a covered Pulumi provider ships, the previous long-term support major reaches end of life on the same day, regardless of how much of its 12-month window remained.
Within the long-term support major of a covered Pulumi provider, only the latest minor version receives patches; earlier minor versions are frozen.
Pulumi provider LTS releases are available through the same standard package registries as current-major releases, but are tagged differently.
Customers pinning a Pulumi provider to a specific major version automatically receive patch releases as they ship, and pinning to a specific major version is the recommended practice.
At any time, exactly one major version of a covered Pulumi provider is the LTS version, and older majors receive no patches.
N is the latest released major version: if v3 is the newest release, then v3 is N, v2 is N−1, and v1 and earlier are end of life.
The current major version (N) of a Pulumi provider receives new features, new resources, bug fixes, security patches, dependency upgrades, and new upstream API versions, until N+1 ships.

The long-term support version (N−1) of a covered Pulumi provider is supported for up to 12 months from N's release, or until N+1 ships, and receives security updates in the provider's code or its direct dependencies.
End-of-life Pulumi provider versions (N−2 and older) are not supported and will not receive updates.
The Pulumi support FAQ page at /docs/support/faq/infrastructure/ has a section on 'What are the best practices for maintaining provider versions'.
Pages exist at /registry/ (Pulumi Registry) and /docs/support/getting-support/ (Getting support).
